check.x: Professionalism
Introduces self and role to Mrs Rao, Mr Rao and the midwives; hand hygiene, gloves and PPE.
Takes the lead calmly with clear closed-loop instructions (for example, who sites the cannulas and who records the blood loss and drugs).
History
Establishes the birth and the bleeding from the midwife:

kids.x: Vaginal birth 25 minutes ago of a 4.3 kg baby after a 16-hour labour augmented with oxytocin
Third stage: oxytocin 10 units IM given, placenta by controlled cord traction 10 minutes ago and not yet checked
Bleeding since the placenta, with the estimated and quantified blood loss

check.x: Asks about pregnancy complications [gestational diabetes on metformin, polyhydramnios, large baby] and previous births [two uncomplicated vaginal births].
Asks about conditions that change drug choice or bleeding risk: asthma, hypertension or pre-eclampsia, bleeding disorders, anticoagulants and allergies, and the blood group [O positive].
Asks when she last passed urine [about 4 hours ago, before pushing].
Examination
Performs a rapid A to E assessment:

kids.x: Airway, breathing and SpO2 [patent, RR 22, chest clear, SpO2 97% on room air]
Circulation: pulse, BP, capillary refill and peripheries [HR 118, BP 98/58, CRT 3 seconds, cool hands and feet]
Disability, glucose and temperature [alert, GCS 15, BGL 6.2 mmol/L, 36.6 °C]

check.x: Asks for the blood loss to be quantified by weighing pads and drapes rather than relying on the visual estimate [1,100 mL and rising].
Palpates the abdomen and finds a soft, boggy fundus above the umbilicus, deviated to the right, and a full bladder.
Inspects the perineum and vagina for trauma [no tear or haematoma; blood and clots coming through the cervix].
Interpretation
Recognises primary PPH (over 1,000 mL) with compensated shock: HR 118, BP 98/58 (shock index about 1.2), CRT 3 seconds and cool peripheries.
Recognises on reassessment that the uterus is still atonic and the bleeding and shock are getting worse: 1,500 mL lost, HR 124, BP 92/56 (shock index about 1.35).
Names uterine atony (Tone) as the most likely cause.
Links atony to her risk factors: an overdistended uterus (4.3 kg baby, polyhydramnios), a long labour augmented with oxytocin (which also blunts the response to further oxytocin) and a full bladder.
Interprets the missing cotyledon with a ragged defect as retained placental tissue (Tissue), which also stops the uterus contracting, and tells the senior obstetrician.
Considers Trauma and Thrombin (coagulopathy), and follows up the coagulation and fibrinogen results.
Management
Resuscitates straight away:

kids.x: Confirms the registrar and anaesthetist are coming and activates the local PPH or massive haemorrhage protocol
Two large-bore cannulas (14 to 16G) with bloods: FBE, group and crossmatch, coagulation including fibrinogen, UEC, and venous gas with lactate
Lies her flat, keeps her warm, gives oxygen and warmed IV fluid, with blood products per protocol if bleeding continues

check.x: Rubs up a contraction with fundal massage and expels the clots, explaining that retained clots distend the uterus and stop it contracting, and gives uterotonics at the same time.
Empties the bladder with an indwelling catheter and monitors hourly urine output.
Gives uterotonics and tranexamic acid per local protocol:

kids.x: Oxytocin IV bolus then infusion, then a second-line agent after checking contraindications (ergometrine is avoided in hypertension and carboprost in asthma; she has neither), or misoprostol if others are unavailable
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, as early as possible and within 3 hours of birth

check.x: Decides early on bimanual compression because the uterus stays soft and bleeding continues despite the first measures, while the other measures continue.
Explains bimanual compression to Mrs Rao before starting:

kids.x: She is bleeding heavily because her womb is not tightening; one hand will go inside the vagina and one on her tummy to squeeze the womb
It will hurt, so pain relief is given; it may slow the bleeding while other treatments work, without promising it will stop it
Asks for her agreement and says they will tell her each step

check.x: Demonstrates bimanual compression correctly on the model:

kids.x: Sterile gloves, and one hand on the abdomen behind the uterus
A closed fist in the anterior vaginal fornix
Compresses the uterus between the two hands and keeps it up until the bleeding is controlled or she is in theatre

check.x: Speaks to Mr Rao in plain language:

kids.x: She is bleeding more than we would like; the team is massaging the womb and giving medicines, and he will be told if she needs theatre
Acknowledges how frightening this is and arranges a midwife or support person to stay with him and the baby

check.x: Plans theatre with the registrar for examination under anaesthesia and removal of the retained tissue, with balloon tamponade or surgical options if bleeding continues, and documents the blood loss and drugs given.
Safety netting

Arranges close observation after theatre in a high dependency area, with a repeat Hb and coagulation, an iron plan, clot prevention once bleeding is controlled, and a debrief with open disclosure for both of them.

Before discharge, tells her in plain words to come straight back or call 000 for heavy bleeding (soaking a pad an hour), large clots, fever, smelly discharge or worsening tummy pain, dizziness or fainting, or calf pain or breathlessness.
Arranges follow-up: GP and midwife review with a blood count, and a plan for any future birth in hospital with active management of the third stage.

desc: This station involves a rapid focused history and examination of a woman bleeding heavily after the birth of a big baby, then interpreting her reassessment and the placenta, managing an atonic postpartum haemorrhage with consented bimanual compression, speaking to her partner, recognising retained placental tissue and safety-netting.
explain:
Uterine atony

Uterine atony is failure of the uterus to contract and retract after birth. It is the most common cause of primary PPH (the Tone of the four Ts: Tone, Tissue, Trauma, Thrombin). Risk factors are precipitate or prolonged labour, an overdistended uterus (macrosomia, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy), grand multiparity and chorioamnionitis. A full bladder also gets in the way of the uterus contracting. Mrs Rao had several of these: a 4.3 kg baby, polyhydramnios, a long labour augmented with oxytocin and a bladder that had not been emptied. Hours of oxytocin infusion also blunt the uterus's response to further oxytocin, so second-line uterotonics are needed early.

Interpreting the findings

On review she has lost more than 1,000 mL and is in compensated shock: HR 118, BP 98/58 (shock index about 1.2), CRT 3 seconds and cool peripheries. Visual estimates under-read blood loss (900 mL estimated, 1,100 mL weighed). On reassessment the uterus is still soft, the loss has reached 1,500 mL and the shock index has risen to about 1.35, so medical measures alone are not enough and bimanual compression and escalation are needed now. A missing cotyledon with a ragged defect on the maternal surface means placental tissue is retained, which stops the uterus contracting well and needs removal under anaesthesia.

Why expel the clots

Retained clots distend the uterus and stop it contracting effectively, which sets up a cycle of more bleeding and more clot. The clots should be expelled by fundal massage (rubbing up a contraction) or removed manually. Uterotonics are still given at the same time. The bladder should be emptied by catheter because a full bladder displaces the fundus upwards and impairs contraction.

Medical management

Resuscitate and treat the cause at the same time. Call for help early and follow the local PPH protocol. Site two large-bore cannulas, take bloods including group and crossmatch and fibrinogen, give warmed crystalloid and blood products as indicated, and measure blood loss by weight rather than estimating it. Escalate uterotonics stepwise, checking contraindications. Typical doses (follow the local protocol): oxytocin 5 units by slow IV injection, then an oxytocin infusion; ergometrine 250 micrograms IM or slow IV, avoided in hypertension, pre-eclampsia and heart disease; carboprost 250 micrograms IM, repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses (2 mg), avoided in asthma; misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually or 800 to 1,000 micrograms rectally. Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible and within 3 hours of birth, with a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours. If bleeding continues, move to theatre early for examination under anaesthesia and removal of the retained tissue with prophylactic antibiotics, then balloon tamponade or surgical options if bleeding persists.

Bimanual compression

Consider it early, with colleagues, if bleeding is heavy from an atonic uterus, and continue other PPH management at the same time. Wear sterile gloves. Place one hand on the abdomen behind the uterus and a closed fist in the anterior vaginal fornix, then compress the uterus between the two hands. Maintain compression until bleeding is controlled or she is in theatre. It is painful, so give analgesia.

Counselling before compression should be brief and honest: she is bleeding heavily because her womb is not tightening; with her agreement you will place one hand in the vagina and one on the tummy to squeeze the womb; it will hurt, so pain relief is being given; it may slow the bleeding while other treatments work; and you will tell her each step. Ask permission and respect her answer where she is able to give it, even in an emergency.

Talking to the partner

A partner watching a PPH is frightened and often feels ignored. Use plain language: she is bleeding more than we would like after the birth and the team is working together to stop it; we are massaging the womb and giving medicines, and I will tell you if she needs to go to theatre. Acknowledge that this is frightening to watch and offer to stay with him and explain what is happening. Make sure a midwife or support person can stay with him and the baby, and follow up with open disclosure and debriefing afterwards.

Safety netting and follow-up

After theatre she needs close observation with repeat Hb and coagulation, an iron plan and VTE prophylaxis once bleeding is controlled. Retained tissue raises the risk of infection and secondary PPH, so before discharge she should be told to come straight back or call 000 for heavy bleeding, large clots, fever, offensive discharge, worsening abdominal pain, dizziness, or calf pain or breathlessness. Follow-up includes GP and midwife review, a debrief, and a plan for any future birth in hospital with active management of the third stage.
focus: Atonic postpartum haemorrhage on the labour ward
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Part 1 is a rapid history and examination; if the candidate starts treatment, the midwife acknowledges it, and it counts when the management is marked in Part 2. If the candidate ordered fundal massage in Part 1, tell them at the reassessment that large clots were expelled and the uterus firmed briefly, then relaxed again. Otherwise the reassessment is a snapshot 5 minutes after the review and is the same whatever was started in Part 1 (a catheter or drug ordered was still being given, so the bladder is still palpable). A high-performing candidate takes the lead, gets the key history quickly (big baby, polyhydramnios, long augmented labour, third birth, oxytocin given, placenta not yet checked, last void 4 hours ago, no asthma or hypertension, blood group), asks for the blood loss to be weighed, and finds compensated shock, a boggy uterus above the umbilicus and a full bladder with no genital tract tear. In Part 2 they recognise that the uterus is still atonic, name atony and the retained cotyledon, and give their management in order: protocol activation, access and bloods, massage and catheter, uterotonics and tranexamic acid, and early bimanual compression. They explain compression to Mrs Rao in plain language, warn her it will hurt, ask her agreement, demonstrate a correct technique (one hand on the abdomen behind the uterus, a fist in the anterior fornix), speak kindly and simply to Mr Rao, plan theatre for the retained tissue, and give specific warning signs and follow-up.

A borderline candidate recognises PPH and calls for help, and may give massage and oxytocin, but misses some of the following: the full bladder, the reason for expelling clots, a complete bimanual technique, a consent discussion before compression, or the significance of the cotyledon defect. Their communication with the partner may be hurried or full of jargon. An unsafe candidate delays escalation, omits IV access and bloods, performs compression without explanation or consent, or misses the retained placental tissue.
patient:
Role: One role-player plays Mrs Anita Rao, a 33-year-old woman on the labour ward bed; she is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. The examiner plays the midwife unless a second role-player is available, and Mr Rao if no one else can. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. If the candidate starts giving treatment orders in Part 1, the midwife says "Noted"; management is marked in Part 2.

Opening line (midwife): "She is still bleeding heavily with clots. I think it is about 900 mL so far."

History from the midwife (give only when asked):

  • Vaginal birth 25 minutes ago of a 4.3 kg baby, after a 16-hour labour augmented with an oxytocin infusion. Afebrile throughout labour.
  • Oxytocin 10 units IM was given with the birth of the baby. The placenta was delivered by controlled cord traction 10 minutes ago. It is in a bowl and has not been checked yet; if the candidate asks to examine it, say it will be handed over shortly (it is given in Part 2).
  • Bright red bleeding with clots since the placenta. Your estimate is 900 mL. If the candidate asks for the pads and drapes to be weighed, the quantified blood loss is 1,100 mL and rising.
  • She last passed urine about 4 hours ago, before pushing.
  • Pregnancy: gestational diabetes managed with diet and metformin; polyhydramnios on ultrasound; baby estimated large for gestational age.
  • Blood group O positive, antibody screen negative.

History from Mrs Rao (give only when asked):

  • This is your third baby. Two previous uncomplicated vaginal births (3.4 kg and 3.7 kg), with no heavy bleeding.
  • No asthma. No high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia. No bleeding problems and no blood thinners. No allergies.
  • Medicines in pregnancy: metformin and a pregnancy multivitamin.

Behaviour (Mrs Rao): pale, anxious and a little light-headed. Say: "I feel a bit dizzy and cold. Is that a lot of blood?" You can follow commands and answer questions. The baby is skin to skin on your chest and is well.

Behaviour (Mr Rao): standing frozen at the bedside, pale, holding the baby's blanket and saying nothing in Part 1. If the candidate uses jargon at any point, say: "I do not understand what that means."
points: Uterine atony (Tone) is the most common cause of primary PPH; risk factors include prolonged or precipitate labour, overdistension (macrosomia, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy), grand multiparity and chorioamnionitis, and a full bladder can impair contraction.
Expel retained clots by fundal massage or manual removal because they distend the uterus and prevent effective contraction, and keep giving uterotonics at the same time.

Consider bimanual compression early: one hand on the abdomen behind the uterus, a fist in the anterior fornix, maintained until bleeding is controlled or she is in theatre, with analgesia and explanation and consent beforehand.
Speak to the partner in plain language, acknowledge how frightening it is and say you will keep them updated.
A missing cotyledon or ragged maternal surface defect suggests retained placental tissue: alert the senior clinician and expect PPH.

World Health Organization. WHO recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage. 2012.
stem: You are the medical resident on call for the labour ward at a metropolitan hospital. The midwife asks you to urgently review Mrs Anita Rao, a 33-year-old woman who gave birth vaginally a short time ago and is bleeding heavily. The obstetric registrar and the anaesthetist have been called and are on their way. A second midwife is in the room, and Mrs Rao's partner, Mr Vikram Rao, is at the bedside. A bimanual compression model is available.
tasks: Take a rapid focused history from Mrs Rao and the midwife and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations on review and on reassessment, and the placenta. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, including explaining bimanual compression to Mrs Rao, gaining her consent and demonstrating it on the model, and speaking to Mr Rao, and give your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Boggy uterus after a big baby

part2.lead: Here are her observations when you arrived and on reassessment 5 minutes later. The midwife now hands you the placenta.

handover.label: Observations on review and on reassessment 5 minutes later
handover.result: Blood loss quantified by weighing pads and drapes. Reassessed at 16:50 while the bleeding continued.
handover.model:
Read: on review HR 118, BP 98/58 (shock index about 1.2), RR 22, SpO2 97% on room air, CRT 3 seconds with cool peripheries, alert, temperature 36.6 °C and BGL 6.2, with a weighed loss of 1,100 mL and rising (the visual estimate of 900 mL under-read it). Five minutes later 1,500 mL, HR 124, BP 92/56 (shock index about 1.35), RR 24, more light-headed, the fundus still soft above the umbilicus and the bladder still full.

Meaning: primary PPH over 1,000 mL with compensated shock that is getting worse. The uterus is still atonic (Tone, the likeliest cause, with a 4.3 kg baby, polyhydramnios and a long oxytocin-augmented labour behind it) despite the first measures, and the full bladder is still in its way; her blood pressure is holding only because she is compensating, and the tachycardia is well beyond the 10 to 20 beat rise of pregnancy.

What it changes: medical measures alone are not enough. Activate the PPH protocol with the registrar and anaesthetist, empty the bladder with a catheter now, keep rubbing up the fundus and escalate uterotonics with tranexamic acid, start bimanual compression with her consent, give blood products, and prepare for theatre; observations at least every 5 minutes.

rows.note: Quantified blood loss 1,100 mL and rising (visual estimate 900 mL)
Blood loss now 1,500 mL; bright red bleeding with clots continues; fundus soft, above the umbilicus; bladder still palpable; more light-headed

handover.label: Placenta and membranes
handover.result:
Placenta delivered by controlled cord traction at 16:35, examined on the trolley at 16:50.

PartFinding
Maternal surfaceOne cotyledon missing, with a ragged defect about 4 cm wide; the remaining cotyledons fit together. No adherent retroplacental clot.
MembranesAmnion and chorion both present and complete. No torn vessels running to the edge of the membranes.
Fetal surfaceNormal
CordThree vessels (two arteries, one vein); central insertion
handover.model:
Read: the maternal surface has a missing cotyledon with a ragged defect about 4 cm wide. The membranes are complete, the cord has three vessels, and no vessels run to the membrane edge, so there is no sign of a succenturiate lobe.

Meaning: placental tissue is retained in the uterus (Tissue). It stops the uterus contracting, adding to the atony (Tone), and raises the risk of ongoing bleeding, infection and secondary PPH.

What it changes: tell the registrar now. Uterotonics and compression will not fix this on their own: she needs theatre for examination under anaesthesia and removal of the retained tissue with antibiotic cover, then balloon tamponade or surgery if bleeding continues. Keep Trauma and Thrombin in mind: the genital tract is checked again under anaesthesia and the coagulation and fibrinogen results followed up.

ask: What do the observations, the reassessment and the placenta show?
What is the most likely cause of the bleeding, and what else must you consider?
What would you do first, and what now that she is still bleeding with a soft uterus? Explain bimanual compression to Mrs Rao, gain her consent and demonstrate it on the model.
Mr Rao says: "There is so much blood. Is she going to die? Nobody is telling me anything." What do you say to him?
What happens next for Mrs Rao, and what safety netting and follow-up does she need?
part2.patient:
In Part 2:

  • If the candidate explains bimanual compression clearly and asks permission, Mrs Rao says: "Yes, please do whatever you need to." If they do not explain or ask, she says: "What are you doing?"
  • Mrs Rao asks: "Will this stop the bleeding? Am I going to need an operation?"
  • Mr Rao says: "There is so much blood. Is she going to die? Nobody is telling me anything." He settles if the candidate acknowledges how frightening this is, explains simply what is happening and offers to keep him updated.
